display_title: High Winter Energy Costs Projected for Britain
display_title_he: תחזית לעלויות אנרגיה גבוהות בבריטניה בחורף
short_summary: Great Britain is anticipated to experience some of Europe's highest energy costs this winter as it pays premium prices for imports. Operators must navigate tight European supplies, low gas storage reserves, and vulnerable power grids.

image.credit: U.S. Energy Information Administration · Public domain

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter

paragraphs: Great Britain is projected to face some of the steepest energy bills in Europe this coming winter, driven by a growing dependence on costly cross-border imports to preserve grid stability. According to official seasonal forecasts, system operators are confident that domestic demand for gas and electricity will be met over the colder months, though achieving this security will largely depend on paying elevated market rates compared to neighboring European nations.

These projections arrive shortly after Europe’s benchmark wholesale gas price reached its highest mark since December 2022, when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine disrupted international energy markets. In response to potential supply shortfalls, National Gas, the operator of Britain’s gas transmission network, negotiated an eleventh-hour agreement with the operator of a critical Belgian pipeline. The deal, formally sanctioned by the regulator Ofgem, reverses an intended capacity reduction and will add approximately 10 pence per month to typical household bills, heading off the risk of shortages under extreme freezing conditions.

Securing physical supply also requires heavier reliance on maritime deliveries. National Gas forecasts that shipments of seaborne liquefied natural gas (LNG) will rise by roughly 5% compared to the previous winter. However, global LNG prices have surged to three times their pre-crisis levels following extensive supply disruptions in the Gulf region linked to Middle Eastern conflicts. Furthermore, European gas storage reserves plunged to their lowest late-summer level in thirteen years by the end of August, depressed by curtailed exports from Qatar and heavy power consumption for refrigeration during scorching summer heatwaves.

The United Kingdom remains uniquely exposed because decades of North Sea extraction led authorities to maintain exceptionally modest gas storage capacity. Although domestic production was projected to decline by 6% relative to last winter, the government’s controversial recent approval of the Jackdaw gasfield could provide a modest supply injection when operations commence next month.

Electricity infrastructure faces parallel vulnerabilities. The National Energy System Operator (Neso) expects Great Britain to remain a net electricity importer throughout the winter, even as continental supplies tighten. Prolonged summer heatwaves depleted European river levels, dampening French nuclear generation and pulling Norwegian hydroelectric reserves below their ten-year minimum since late July. Over the twelve months ending in August, Britain spent a record £4bn on power imports, with half directed toward France, according to figures released by the Office for National Statistics.

Compounding these expenses, grid bottlenecks have repeatedly forced grid operators to pay wind and solar facilities to curtail generation, while simultaneously issuing near-record payouts to start up fossil-fueled gas turbines. Although overall gas combustion for electricity generation is projected to decline due to expanding renewable capacity, National Gas noted that gas demand during acute supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously estimated. As Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, observed, tightening supply margins will test system flexibility whenever freezing, sunless, and windless winter weather depresses renewable generation.

facts.fact: Great Britain is expected to pay some of Europe's highest energy costs this winter due to an increasing reliance on gas and electricity imports.
Official energy forecasts show that Great Britain will secure enough energy to meet winter demand in part by paying higher wholesale prices than neighboring markets.
National Gas agreed to an eleventh-hour deal with a Belgian pipeline operator to maintain gas flows, approved by Ofgem and adding around 10p per month to average household bills.
Seaborne LNG imports to Britain are forecast to rise by about 5% from last winter, with market prices three times higher than before the Middle East crisis disrupted Gulf supplies.
European gas storage reserves reached a 13-year low for late August due to curtailed Qatari exports and high summer cooling demand during heatwaves.
UK North Sea gas output was forecast to fall 6% year-on-year, though the recently approved Jackdaw gasfield is expected to provide a modest supply boost when it begins operating next month.
Great Britain is forecast to be a net importer of electricity this winter, after spending a record £4bn on power imports in the year to August, half of which went to France.
Low river levels in Europe have reduced French nuclear output and kept Norwegian hydroelectric reserves below their 10-year minimum since late July.
Gas power demand during extreme supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed because of dark, windless winter weather.
